answer: The authors recorded neural activity using in vivo two-photon calcium imaging with a Fidelity-2 1070 nm laser and a 16× objective, capturing movies at 15 frames/s. The calcium sensor was the genetically encoded indicator jRGECO1a, delivered via a retrograde AAV vector (AAV-Syn-jRGECO1a) injected into CA3 to label mature dentate gyrus neurons, as direct labeling of immature adult-born neurons was unsuccessful. Behaviorally, mice were head-fixed on a motorized treadmill with four distinct textures (velvet, smooth, sandpaper) and an optical rotary encoder/RFID tags to track position. To quantify spatial coding, they calculated single-cell Fisher Information (FI) using unfiltered ΔF/F traces and a discrimination threshold (minimum distance for 70% correct discrimination). Population spatial information was assessed by decoding position via logistic regression on unfiltered fluorescence traces, yielding d-prime squared (linear Fisher information). Single-cell tuning was measured as the modulus of a normalized tuning vector derived from deconvolved, thresholded firing rates.
